clue.text: Dispatcher bullish about his work

parts.note: a dispatcher is one who kills, and the bullfighter's work is all about bulls, so 'bullish' is literal rather than meaning optimistic

explanation.surface: A keen shipping clerk is upbeat about his job.
explanation.definitionFit: The bullfighter who delivers the killing stroke in the ring dispatches the bull, his whole trade revolving around it.

clue.text: Appropriately, what the stones made

parts.note: the Rolling Stones band played a genre named, fittingly, after stones themselves

explanation.surface: A remark on what some stones produced, fittingly.
explanation.definitionFit: The Rolling Stones are a famous guitar band whose genre of popular songs carries a word for stone in its name.

clue.text: Stars of us space programme

explanation.surface: Celebrities from an American space project.
explanation.definitionFit: The Twins constellation of zodiac stars shares its name with NASA's 1960s two-man spaceflight programme.

clue.text: Applaud trick that's a bit of nonsense

parts.note: to applaud is to clap the hands
a trick or snare is a trap

explanation.surface: Clapping at a con trick is a little silly.
explanation.definitionFit: Pretentious empty talk is a synonym for drivel or rubbish.

clue.text: Succeed, not trespassing on alien territory

explanation.surface: Someone thrives by keeping off land that belongs to others.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom means to flourish or be fully recognised; read literally it is entering land that is yours, so no trespass occurs.

clue.text: Not knowing cost, gain on exchange

indicators.note: letters swapped about, as goods are on an exchange, signal that cost and gain are rearranged

explanation.surface: Unsure of the price, a profit made on the stock exchange.
explanation.walkthrough: 'on exchange' sounds like trading, but it rearranges COST and GAIN.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone of this view holds that the existence of God cannot be known, from Greek for without knowledge.

clue.text: Food in stomach

explanation.surface: Something to eat sitting in the belly.
explanation.definitionFit: Cooked cow's stomach lining is a traditional British dish, so the word names both the food and the organ.

clue.text: First class, the French man, but gets in a flap on planes

parts.note: A1 means first-class, written here as the letters A and I
le is French for the
Ron is a man's name

explanation.surface: A top-notch French chap nonetheless panics aboard aircraft.
explanation.walkthrough: A1 (first-rate) is taken as AI. 'gets in a flap' looks like panic but leads to the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: This hinged control surface on an aircraft wing is a movable flap used to roll the plane.

clue.text: Father will take part, word of honour

parts.note: pa is an informal word for father
a part in a play is a role

explanation.surface: Dad promises to accept a role in the play.
explanation.definitionFit: A prisoner's release on promise of good behaviour comes from French for word, the pledge given.

clue.text: Chap at helm, say, has head cover

indicators.note: say signals that the phrase is spoken and the spelling of the answer follows the sound

parts.note: a chap is a man and the steering lever at a boat's helm is a tiller

explanation.surface: A man steering a boat wears a hat.
explanation.walkthrough: MAN plus TILLER, said aloud in a non-rhotic accent, gives the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: A lace scarf worn over the hair and shoulders, especially in Spain, covers the head.

clue.text: Make no progress in notice period

parts.note: to notice or observe is to mark
a period is a span of time

explanation.surface: Stalling during the period of notice before leaving a job.
explanation.walkthrough: 'notice period' reads as the time before leaving a job; here the words separate.
explanation.definitionFit: Soldiers marching on the spot without advancing do this, hence the idiom for treading water.

clue.text: Drink for Mrs Blair, we hear

indicators.note: we hear signals that the sound of the words matters, not their spelling

parts.note: Cherie Blair is the wife of former UK prime minister Tony Blair

explanation.surface: A glass offered to the former prime minister's wife.
explanation.definitionFit: A fortified wine from southern Spain is a drink.

clue.text: Mixing in with water could be the answer

explanation.surface: Stirring something into water might solve the problem.
explanation.definitionFit: A liquid in which something is dissolved, and also the answer to a puzzle or problem.

clue.text: Henry VIII was not using brain

parts.note: the famously stout Tudor monarch was not slim, so 'was not' points to the quality he lacked: thin
Henry VIII was a king of England

explanation.surface: A jibe that the Tudor monarch was brainless.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue reads as a jibe that Henry VIII was brainless, but it really says the portly king was no THIN KING. Split the answer in two to see it.
explanation.definitionFit: Applying the mind or reasoning means using one's brain.

clue.text: Dissolved early link to Irish town

indicators.note: dissolved means broken up, so the letters of early and link are rearranged

explanation.surface: An early connection to an Irish town was severed.
explanation.definitionFit: A town in County Kerry famed for its lakes is in the south-west of Ireland.

clue.text: Take crack up to a union needing drug

parts.note: to crack up is to praise highly, as in all it is cracked up to be, so laud
NUM is the National Union of Mineworkers in Britain

explanation.surface: Accepting crack ahead of a union deal that needs narcotics.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Take' is an instruction to join LAUD to A and NUM; 'crack' is not the drug here. NUM is Britain's National Union of Mineworkers.
explanation.definitionFit: Opium dissolved in alcohol was a widely used Victorian painkiller and narcotic.

clue.text: Detached from the scoring

parts.note: in a musical score, notes marked as detached are played short and separated

explanation.surface: Cut off from the points being tallied in a game.
explanation.definitionFit: An Italian musical direction marks notes to be played short and separate from one another.

clue.text: One who's behind a short film

explanation.surface: Whoever is responsible for a brief movie.
explanation.definitionFit: One lagging or following behind, and a short preview advertising a forthcoming film.

clue.text: One giving corroboration? That's the ticket

explanation.surface: Someone backing up a claim declares it just right.
explanation.definitionFit: One who vouches for something confirms it, and a coupon or token exchanged for goods is a ticket.

clue.text: Reportedly a bony old emperor

parts.note: British cartoons and newspapers called the French ruler Boney, as if he were thin

explanation.surface: Accounts describe a skinny former monarch.
explanation.definitionFit: The French emperor Bonaparte was nicknamed Boney in contemporary British reports.

clue.text: Collect type of truck

explanation.surface: Fetching a particular sort of lorry.
explanation.definitionFit: To collect someone in a car, and a light open-backed truck.

clue.text: Such gentry experienced a come down?

explanation.surface: Aristocrats who have suffered a fall in fortune.
explanation.definitionFit: Landowning gentry in Britain, and an aircraft or jumper that has touched down.

clue.text: Below cost, sells poor spirits

explanation.surface: A shop sells cheap alcohol at a loss.
explanation.definitionFit: Selling goods abroad at below cost price, and the low mood of someone down in the doldrums.

clue.text: A win in this event is in the bag

definitions.text: A win in this event is in the bag

parts.words: A win in this event is in the bag
parts.note: in the bag usually means certain, but in this school sports race the competitors literally hop along inside bags

explanation.surface: Victory in this contest is guaranteed.
explanation.definitionFit: A school sports-day race in which competitors jump forward with their legs in sacks.

clue.text: Ruddy duck? Another bird

parts.note: ruddy and flaming are both mild British intensifiers, like bloody
a duck is a score of nought in cricket, so O

explanation.surface: Asking whether a red-faced waterfowl is a different bird.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ruddy duck' is a real bird, but here it splits as FLAMING plus O (a duck being a zero score in cricket).
explanation.definitionFit: A pink long-legged wading bird is another bird after the ruddy duck.

clue.text: Irregular to have a French archdeacon

parts.note: une is French for a (feminine)
Ven, short for Venerable, is the title given to an archdeacon

explanation.surface: Odd for a French church official to be present.
explanation.walkthrough: Archdeacons in the Church of England are styled the Venerable, abbreviated Ven.
explanation.definitionFit: Something not smooth or regular is bumpy or unequal.

clue.text: Cheeky chap just starting course

parts.note: fresh can mean impudent or cheeky
a chap is a man

explanation.surface: An impudent fellow is new to the course.
explanation.definitionFit: A first-year university student has only just begun a degree.
